newsitem.title: USA: 'Significant' gap seen in U.S.-Japan insurance talks.
newsitem.headline: 'Significant' gap seen in U.S.-Japan insurance talks.

text.p: U.S. trade negotiator Ira Shapiro said there were still significant differences between Washington and Tokyo on how to open up Japan's giant insurance market despite hours of talks on Friday.

"We've had a good meeting, but differences are still significant," Shapiro told reporters as the first day of a two-day negotiating session ended. "We're going to meet again tomorrow morning to continue discussions."
Shapiro and Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, are leading the negotiations.
Sakakibara said he expected no quick breakthrough.

"We would at least want to agree on a timetable, but like I said before I left Tokyo, there won't be a conclusion at this round, much less tonight," Sakakibara said during a break in the late-night session.
Shapiro earlier said the talks had so far been "useful" but declined to elaborate.

At issue is Japan's $382 billion domestic insurance market. Washington is pressing Japan to liberalize its primary insurance markets before a niche area called the "Third Sector," where U.S. firms have been dominant, is opened up to Japanese insurers.
The Third Sector includes areas such as personal accident, illness and nursing care, and stand-alone cancer policies.
Earlier on Friday, Sakakibara told reporters that U.S. and Japanese negotiators were still looking for a way to resolve differences in opening up Japan's insurance market.
Sakakibara said the meeting was basically groundwork for further talks at the ministerial level, possibly at the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation forum meeting later this month.

Asked if Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's recently unveiled financial deregulation plan -- dubbed Big Bang after the 1986 British reforms -- would mandate a total liberalization, Sakakibara said consistency was "an issue."

A U.S. official in San Francisco said the United States would make "strong efforts" to reach an agreement at this meeting. "The United States is entering into these talks with the intention of making strong efforts to reach a resolution and we intend to work hard toward that goal," he said.

The United States wants Japan to live up to a 1994 agreement that calls for deregulation of the primary sector dominated by big Japanese firms before deregulation of the so-called third sector of specialty insurance.

On Thursday, a U.S. trade official in Washington expressed doubt that the dispute would be fully resolved in these talks. He said the "ball is substantially in Japan's court" because Tokyo removed a number of primary sector issues from the table during negotiations in September.
The two sides have set a deadline of Dec. 15 to resolve their differences.
